title: Public support for CEO activism is becoming more issue-specific, while executive speech increasingly enters consumer choice and corporate legitimacy
source_unit: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Rock Center for Corporate Governance and Hoover Institution, 2026 CEO Activism Survey, September 2026
geography: United States; adults nationally, with demographic, partisan, age and issue comparisons

observations.period: Summer 2026; public support for CEO activism across issue domains

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in nationwide survey representative by gender, race, age, household income and region

overall_support.value: public support for CEOs taking public positions declines relative to the 2018 follow-up baseline

issue_specificity.value: support remains stronger for environmental advocacy and weaker for political and contentious social advocacy

cross_group_direction.value: support falls across age groups and political affiliations and for almost every issue

observations.method: Nationwide survey conducted in summer 2026 as a follow-up to Stanford's 2018 CEO activism survey; public page reports directional findings but not the full 2026 crosstab tables.
observations.uncertainty: The accessible release does not provide all issue-level percentages, question wording or fieldwork vendor details; cross-wave changes may reflect issue context, political events, sample or measurement differences.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults by age, party affiliation, gender, race, household income and region.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower support for CEO speech does not necessarily mean lower concern about the underlying issues; it may reflect skepticism about corporate authority, politicization or perceived competence.

observations.period: Summer 2026; age-specific caution around CEO advocacy on artificial intelligence

younger_AI_caution.value: younger Americans are more cautious about CEO advocacy concerning artificial intelligence

corporate_AI_voice.value: CEO speech about AI is treated as an issue of corporate legitimacy rather than automatically trusted expertise

observations.method: Survey comparison of public responses to CEO activism across environmental, social, political and AI-related issues.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not show the size of the age gap or distinguish whether caution reflects job risk, privacy, product exposure, political polarization or distrust of corporate motives.
observations.subgroup: Younger U.S. adults compared with older adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: Caution may coexist with demand for corporate responsibility; rejecting CEO advocacy as a voice does not imply rejecting firm-level AI safeguards or accountability.

observations.period: Summer 2026; consumer memory and purchase response to CEO activism

behavior_change.value: consumers report increasingly changing purchasing behavior in response to CEO activism

lasting_recall.value: Americans show hypersensitivity to and lasting recall of CEO activism, with both positive and negative reactions

market_mechanism.value: executive speech can become a consumer-choice and corporate-reputation signal beyond the firm's products or services

observations.method: Survey questions about remembered CEO activism and self-reported changes in purchasing behavior, compared with the 2018 survey.
observations.uncertainty: Self-reported purchase change is not verified transaction data; the public summary does not report effect size, persistence, product category or whether negative and positive responses are symmetric.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers, with differences expected by political identity, age and issue alignment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Recall and stated purchase response may be concentrated among politically engaged consumers and may not translate into aggregate sales or durable brand switching.

institutional_role.value: the 2026 study revisits whether CEOs should use corporate authority to speak on environmental, social and political issues

legitimacy_boundary.value: public acceptance of CEO speech is increasingly conditional on issue, identity, generation and perceived corporate role

observations.method: Follow-up survey design intended to compare public views of CEO activism with the 2018 Stanford survey.
observations.uncertainty: The public landing pages do not provide the complete instrument or full cross-wave tables, so this record preserves the direction and mechanism rather than estimating a precise trend magnitude.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, consumers, corporate leaders and boards as the institutional audience.
observations.counterinterpretation: Conditional legitimacy can still permit strong corporate action when advocacy is tied to business operations, employee conditions, product safety or environmental effects rather than symbolic political positioning.

related_sources.claim: Stanford GSB publication page describing the survey sample, follow-up design and key findings.

boundary: This record treats CEO activism as a corporate-legitimacy and consumer-response signal. It does not establish that public speech changes actual sales, employee behavior, political outcomes or social conditions; several 2026 findings are preserved directionally because the full tables are not publicly accessible.
